options.text: Use prediction ID to retrieve: input features from logs, prediction output, explainability attributions (which features influenced prediction), model version used, timestamp. Compare with similar predictions. Check feature values for anomalies. Use Explainable AI to understand model reasoning. Compare attributions with training-time expectations.
Individual prediction debugging impossible—only aggregate analysis.
Must retrain entire model to fix one wrong prediction.
Wrong predictions can't be investigated—black box limitation.

explanation: A is correct because prediction logging with explainability enables detailed debugging of individual predictions. B is not correct because per-prediction debugging is supported with proper logging—key debugging capability. C is not correct because individual wrong predictions don't require retraining—may be data issue or edge case. D is not correct because explainability tools make models inspectable—not black boxes with proper tooling.

question_text: How do you track throughput (predictions per second) and alert when it deviates from expected patterns?

options.text: Cloud Monitoring tracks prediction_count metric. Compute predictions/second rate. Establish baseline patterns (hourly/daily/weekly). Use anomaly detection or threshold alerts. Alert if throughput drops suddenly (potential issue) or spikes unexpectedly (load surge, abuse). Correlate with traffic patterns and business events.
Throughput monitoring not available—request count only.
Throughput changes don't matter—only latency important.
Throughput always constant—anomaly detection unnecessary.

explanation: A is correct because throughput monitoring with pattern recognition detects traffic anomalies. B is not correct because prediction counts enable rate calculation—throughput derivable from counts. C is not correct because throughput important for capacity planning and issue detection—complements latency. D is not correct because throughput varies with usage patterns—anomaly detection adds value.

question_text: Your recommendation model needs monitoring for diversity and filter bubble effects. What metrics track this?

options.text: Track: recommendation diversity (unique items recommended / total items), coverage (% of catalog recommended), popularity bias (distribution of item popularity in recommendations vs catalog), user exploration (new vs repeated recommendations), category distribution. Monitor trends over time. Alert if diversity drops or bias increases.
Diversity monitoring not applicable to ML—subjective concept.
Filter bubbles can't be measured—only observed anecdotally.
Recommendation systems don't need diversity—relevance only.

explanation: A is correct because diversity metrics enable monitoring for filter bubbles and recommendation quality. B is not correct because diversity is quantifiable with metrics—catalog coverage, uniqueness, distributions. C is not correct because filter bubbles measurable via recommendation patterns—quantitative analysis possible. D is not correct because diversity matters for user experience and discovery—relevance not only metric.

question_text: How do you monitor for data leakage in production (target information leaking into features)?

options.text: Monitor for suspiciously high accuracy or confidence on certain patterns. Use explainability to check if model relies heavily on features that shouldn't be predictive. Check for temporal leakage (future information). Monitor feature-target correlations in production data. Alert on perfect or near-perfect predictions (suspicious).
Data leakage only occurs during training—impossible in production.
Leakage detection requires manual code review—can't automate monitoring.
Perfect predictions are good—not suspicious.

explanation: A is correct because suspicious patterns and attribution analysis can signal production data leakage. B is not correct because leakage can occur in production pipelines—feature engineering bugs at serving time. C is not correct because leakage signals are monitorable—suspicious accuracy patterns, attributions. D is not correct because perfect predictions often indicate leakage—deserve investigation not celebration.

question_text: How do you implement monitoring dashboards that non-technical stakeholders can understand?

options.text: Focus on business metrics: prediction volume, accuracy trends (if available), cost per prediction, uptime %, business KPI impact. Use visualizations: line charts for trends, gauges for health, tables for summaries. Avoid jargon—use plain language. Color coding (green/yellow/red). Stakeholder-specific views. Add context/annotations.
Technical dashboards only—stakeholders don't need monitoring access.
All dashboards must show raw technical metrics—no simplification.
Non-technical stakeholders can't understand any monitoring data.

explanation: A is correct because business-focused metrics with clear visualization enable stakeholder understanding. B is not correct because stakeholder visibility important for alignment—should have appropriate dashboards. C is not correct because simplification and business context make dashboards more valuable—not dumbing down. D is not correct because proper visualization and metrics selection makes monitoring accessible—underestimating stakeholders.

question_text: Your NLP model's predictions need monitoring for toxicity or bias that wasn't caught in training. How do you monitor this?

options.text: Sample predictions periodically. Run through toxicity detection API (Perspective API, Cloud Natural Language). Log toxicity scores. Monitor: toxicity rate over time, toxic predictions by category, severity distribution. Alert if toxicity rate increases. Manual review of flagged predictions. Use separate bias detection for protected attributes.
Toxicity monitoring not possible—requires human judgment only.
If model passed training evaluation, production monitoring unnecessary.
NLP models can't generate toxic content—inherently safe.

explanation: A is correct because toxicity APIs and sampling enable automated content safety monitoring. B is not correct because toxicity APIs provide automated assessment—not purely human judgment. C is not correct because production can surface issues missed in training—continuous monitoring needed. D is not correct because NLP models absolutely can generate problematic content—safety monitoring critical.

question_text: How do you monitor model staleness (how old is the training data relative to production data)?

options.text: Track model metadata: training_data_end_date, model_deployment_date. Compute staleness = current_date - training_data_end_date. Monitor staleness metric. Set thresholds by model type (fraud detection: 30 days, product recommendation: 90 days). Alert when staleness exceeds threshold. Correlate with accuracy decline.
Model staleness doesn't exist—models timeless once trained.
Staleness monitoring requires comparing all features—too complex.
Models never go stale—retraining is unnecessary.

explanation: A is correct because tracking training data age enables staleness monitoring and retraining triggers. B is not correct because models do become stale as world evolves—not timeless. C is not correct because simple date comparison provides staleness metric—not complex. D is not correct because most models require periodic retraining—staleness is real phenomenon.

question_text: Your fraud detection model has class imbalance (99% legitimate, 1% fraud). How do you monitor performance for the minority class?

options.text: Track per-class metrics separately: fraud recall/precision, legitimate recall/precision. Monitor confusion matrix: false negatives (missed fraud), false positives (legitimate flagged). Alert on fraud recall drops. Overall accuracy misleading—can be 99% by predicting all legitimate. Use F1-score for fraud class.
Overall accuracy sufficient—class-specific metrics unnecessary.
Imbalanced data can't be monitored—metrics meaningless.
Minority class too small to monitor—focus on majority only.

explanation: A is correct because per-class metrics essential for imbalanced scenarios—overall accuracy hides minority performance. B is not correct because overall accuracy misleading with imbalance—need class-specific metrics. C is not correct because imbalanced data is monitorable with appropriate metrics—confusion matrix, F1-score. D is not correct because minority class often most important (fraud detection)—critical to monitor.

question_text: How do you implement synthetic monitoring (canary requests) for ML models?

options.text: Create synthetic test cases with known expected outputs. Schedule Cloud Function to send test requests to endpoint periodically (every 5 min). Validate predictions match expectations. Monitor: test success rate, response time, correctness. Alert if tests fail. Use diverse test cases covering edge cases. Tests act as continuous smoke tests.
Synthetic monitoring not applicable to ML—only for web services.
Synthetic tests interfere with production—forbidden.
Real user traffic sufficient—synthetic monitoring redundant.

explanation: A is correct because synthetic monitoring with known test cases enables proactive issue detection. B is not correct because synthetic monitoring applies to ML models—validates availability and correctness. C is not correct because synthetic tests are small overhead and provide value—standard monitoring practice. D is not correct because synthetic monitoring detects issues before user impact—proactive vs reactive.

question_text: Your time-series forecasting model needs monitoring for changing temporal patterns. What specific monitoring do you implement?

options.text: Monitor: forecast accuracy by horizon (1-day, 7-day, 30-day ahead), prediction residuals distribution, seasonal pattern changes, trend shifts, autocorrelation structure changes. Compare forecast errors over time. Alert if accuracy degrades for specific horizons. Retrain when patterns shift significantly.
Time-series monitoring same as classification—no special considerations.
Temporal patterns can't be monitored—too complex.
Forecasting accuracy impossible to measure in production.

explanation: A is correct because time-series models require temporal-specific monitoring—horizon accuracy, seasonality, trends. B is not correct because time-series has unique characteristics—different monitoring needs than classification. C is not correct because temporal patterns monitorable with statistical methods—standard time-series analysis. D is not correct because forecasting accuracy measurable by comparing predictions to actual outcomes—standard evaluation.

question_text: How do you monitor for model backdoors or poisoning attacks in production?

options.text: Monitor for: unusual activation patterns on specific input patterns (backdoor triggers), clusters of similar misclassifications, anomalous attributions (unexpected features driving predictions), predictions inconsistent with similar inputs. Use outlier detection on activations/gradients. Requires deep monitoring of model internals.
Backdoor detection impossible without access to training data.
Production models can't be poisoned—training-time threat only.
Backdoor monitoring requires classified security tools unavailable.

explanation: A is correct because behavioral patterns and activation analysis can signal backdoor presence. B is not correct because backdoor detection uses behavioral signals from production—not training data access. C is not correct because deployed poisoned model exhibits backdoor behavior—detectable in production. D is not correct because backdoor detection uses standard ML techniques—anomaly detection, activation analysis.

question_text: Your model makes millions of predictions daily. How do you efficiently sample predictions for detailed monitoring without losing critical signals?

options.text: Use stratified sampling: always log high-value predictions (high confidence extremes, low confidence predictions, detected anomalies). Random sample rest (1-10%). Use reservoir sampling for stream. Ensure coverage of all segments/categories. Log more during canary deployments. Critical predictions always logged.
Random sampling only—stratification adds complexity.
Must log everything—sampling loses critical information.
Sample first N predictions of day—simplest approach.

explanation: A is correct because stratified sampling ensures important predictions logged while controlling volume. B is not correct because stratification captures critical cases—worth the complexity for better signal. C is not correct because smart sampling preserves signals while reducing volume—not everything needed. D is not correct because temporal sampling biases toward specific times—stratified more representative.

question_text: How do you implement monitoring that detects when model behavior violates business rules or regulatory constraints?

options.text: Implement business rule validation layer: check predictions against constraints (e.g., lending: approve_rate by protected_class within fairness threshold, prices: margin > minimum). Log violations. Alert on violation rate. Block predictions violating hard constraints. Generate compliance reports. Regular audits of rule violations.
Models always comply with rules—validation unnecessary.
Business rules can't be programmatically checked—manual only.
Monitoring and compliance are separate—no integration needed.

explanation: A is correct because programmatic rule validation with monitoring enables compliance tracking and enforcement. B is not correct because models can violate rules—validation essential for regulatory compliance. C is not correct because many business rules are codifiable—automated checking feasible. D is not correct because monitoring should track compliance—integrated approach more effective.

question_text: Your organization has 100+ models. How do you implement monitoring that scales while maintaining model-specific customization?

options.text: Create monitoring framework: base monitoring (latency, errors, throughput) for all models automatically. Model-specific config files (YAML) defining custom metrics, thresholds, baselines. Monitoring templates by model type (classification, regression, recommendation). Centralized dashboard with drill-down. Automated monitoring deployment via CI/CD.
100+ models require 100+ separate monitoring systems—no shared infrastructure.
Scaling monitoring means removing customization—standardization only.
Beyond 50 models, monitoring becomes impractical—reduce model count.

explanation: A is correct because framework approach with config-driven customization enables scale plus flexibility. B is not correct because shared monitoring infrastructure with per-model config scales better—not separate systems. C is not correct because framework enables both scale and customization—not mutually exclusive. D is not correct because monitoring frameworks designed for hundreds of models—not impractical with automation.

question_text: Your computer vision model processes images. How do you monitor for distribution shift in image data?

options.text: Monitor: image statistics (brightness, contrast distributions), embedding drift (compare embeddings from intermediate layers to training embeddings), prediction confidence distributions, detected object categories distribution. Sample images for manual review. Alert on statistical distribution changes. Use dimensionality reduction (PCA) on embeddings.
Image drift undetectable—images too high-dimensional.
Vision models immune to distribution shift—robust by design.
Must manually review all images—automated monitoring impossible.

explanation: A is correct because image statistics and embedding analysis enable automated image distribution monitoring. B is not correct because embeddings and statistics reduce dimensionality—drift detectable. C is not correct because vision models definitely affected by distribution shift—lighting, quality, content changes. D is not correct because automated statistical analysis scales—manual review for samples only.

question_text: How do you implement post-deployment A/B test analysis comparing champion model to challenger across multiple dimensions?

options.text: Multi-dimensional analysis: 1) Prediction accuracy (if labels available) 2) Business KPIs (revenue, conversions) 3) Latency percentiles 4) Cost per prediction 5) User satisfaction proxies 6) Segment-level performance. Statistical tests: t-test for continuous, chi-squared for categorical. Min sample size calculations. Sequential testing for early stopping.
A/B analysis only needs accuracy—single metric sufficient.
Statistical tests unnecessary—just compare averages.
Multi-dimensional analysis too complex—choose single winner metric.

explanation: A is correct because comprehensive A/B analysis requires multiple dimensions and statistical rigor. B is not correct because holistic comparison includes accuracy, business metrics, performance, cost—not just accuracy. C is not correct because statistical tests provide confidence in results—not just point estimates. D is not correct because multi-dimensional analysis reveals trade-offs—single metric misses important factors.

question_text: Your ML platform serves models for different business units with varying SLAs. How do you implement monitoring that respects different service level requirements?

options.text: Model-level SLO definitions: tag models with service tier (critical/standard/research). Per-tier SLOs: critical (P99 < 50ms, 99.9% uptime, drift checks hourly), standard (P99 < 200ms, 99% uptime, drift daily), research (best effort). Separate alert policies by tier. Dashboard showing per-tier SLO compliance. SLI/SLO tracking.
One SLA for all models—standardization required for monitoring.
Differentiated SLAs impossible to monitor—too complex.
Business unit SLAs don't apply to ML—technical metrics only.

explanation: A is correct because tier-based SLO configuration enables differentiated monitoring aligned with business needs. B is not correct because different business requirements need different SLAs—one-size-fits-all inadequate. C is not correct because tier-based SLOs are standard pattern—metadata-driven configuration enables this. D is not correct because ML services should have SLAs—business expectations apply to ML systems too.
